# TASK: BUILD "THE KEEPER'S LEDGER" — THE FLAGSHIP GAME
# Source: ALL_REMAINING_PLAN.md ITEM 4 (verbatim structure) + verified resources
# From: Runner (runner role: provide, verify — per Owner's operating model)

You are the 7-seat game-build roster, working as one crew:
- gamedesigner (LEAD — owns the build, the sequence, the delivery)
- game_director (vision, tone, what the game is about)
- game_level_content_designer (island arcs, keeper traces, event content)
- game_visual_direction (art direction, look, lighting mood)
- game_performance_engineer (frame budget, the 30fps reality on a T1000)
- game_balance_economist (the duty economy, storm difficulty curves)
- game_qa_critic (the 8.5 judgment — you are the gate)

========================================================================
## THE GAME — "THE KEEPER'S LEDGER"
========================================================================

THE PREMISE:
You are the last keeper of a lighthouse on a remote, storm-ravaged
island. Your light is the only thing keeping ships off the rocks —
and it is dying. The keepers before you vanished, one by one, and
nobody will say why. The supply boat stopped coming months ago.

THE LOOP:
Each night-cycle a storm rolls in, procedurally — different wind,
different rain, different fury. By day you work: feed the flame,
salvage parts from the wrecks that wash ashore, repair the lens
system, ration the oil, keep the log. Ships pass in the night. Some
see your beam and live. Some don't.

WHY THE PREVIOUS KEEPERS VANISHED — the story is not told to you,
it is CAUSED BY YOU:
The island keeps their traces — a ledger page, a rusted lantern, a
note in the lens room. Each keeper's record you find shows what they
neglected, and what it cost. The story advances on YOUR competence:
the lens you clean sets the beam's reach in fog; the oil you
rationed last week decides whether the light survives tonight; the
wreck you failed to report becomes the reef that sinks a ship later.
Neglect compounds. So does care.

THE ENDINGS BRANCH ON YOUR RECORD:
The game keeps an auditable log of every duty done or skipped —
your keeper record. The inspector who finally arrives reads it the
way the island does. Ships saved or sunk, storms ridden out or
suffered, the truth about the vanished keepers assembled or missed —
the ending you get is the one your record earned. No dialogue
choices. The job is the story.

THE ISLAND REMEMBERS:
Wrecks accumulate. Storm damage persists. Paths erode. New dangers
surface where past failures happened. The island permanently
changes — every playthrough's island tells the history of that
playthrough's keeper.

WHAT IT IS NOT: no combat, no enemy AI to build badly, no monsters.
The antagonist is the storm, the dark, and the sea — and your own
record.

========================================================================
## THE BAR — WHY THIS BEATS THE 8 GAMES ALREADY ON THE MARKET
========================================================================
(mined from real player reviews, re-verified Oct 17 with fresh web
research — the complaints below are VERIFIED with sources in the plan)

1. "Mechanics are decoration" — VERIFIED (Ironbark Lookout / Static
   Dread reviews: survival mechanics "completely pointless and affect
   nothing").
   -> YOUR FIX: every duty has mechanical weight. Lens = beam range;
   oil rationing = storm survival; reporting = future reefs. Nothing
   is decorative, and no purchasable item can switch the core loop off.

2. "Repetitive monotony" — VERIFIED ("dull monotony", "very very
   repetitive annoying running around").
   -> YOUR FIX: procedural storms + the remembering island mutate the
   loop every cycle; last cycle's failures physically change this
   cycle's job.

3. "Story makes no sense / tonally inconsistent / reveals too early"
   — VERIFIED ("the story made zero sense to me").
   -> YOUR FIX: the vanished-keepers mystery is assembled from records
   and from the player's own failures — the story emerges from the
   sim, so it cannot be inconsistent with it.

4. "Too short / anemic near the end" — VERIFIED ("falls off and feels
   anemic near the end").
   -> YOUR FIX: endings branch on the keeper record assembled across
   ALL cycles — the endgame is the payoff of the whole record, not a
   scripted cutscene.

5. "Cheap AI content breaks immersion" — VERIFIED ("soulless AI
   voice", "undisclosed GenAI", "AI artwork, sound effects").
   -> YOUR FIX: sound is synthesized (studio v3, real DSP), visuals
   are procedural code (no AI-image slop), and the zero-error bar
   (crash = failed build) is a gate, not a hope.

THE PRECEDENT THAT PROVES THE DESIGN:
Papers, Please — Lucas Pope, built alone, deliberately ugly, no
cinematics: sold beyond projection in a month, IGF Grand Prize,
BAFTA-nominated. The lesson the whole press repeated: "mechanics
carry the meaning... you live in the world your decisions produced."
THAT is the bar: the job produces the world, and the record decides
the ending. The keeper genre has the atmosphere and the audience —
but no game in it has made the job mechanically matter. That seat
is still empty. You are filling it.

========================================================================
## YOUR SEQUENCE (from the plan's full flow)
========================================================================

STEP 1 — UE5 VERIFY (already running):
A UE5.8.3 scalability test is in flight on the T1000 right now
(1080p, medium, volumetric fog + storms; PASS = >= 30fps on the test
scene). Its result decides your engine: PASS = Unreal; FAIL = Godot 4
stylized (documented decision). Check its outcome before Step 3.

STEP 2 — SPEC LOCK (your first work):
Write the full design doc BEFORE building anything: systems,
keeper-record mechanics, storm/lens/oil interactions, island layout,
endings, critic rubric. Brief-first law — the design exists on disk
before code does. FROM YOUR DESIGN, derive the complete asset list:
which character, which animations, which props. The plan's note
"Mixamo rig: walk/run/climb/row, provenance noted" is PROVISIONAL —
you decide what the design actually needs and where each asset comes
from. Provenance noted for every downloaded asset.

STEP 3 — BLENDER ASSET PHASE:
Drive Blender's Python API to build: procedural island + coastline,
lighthouse (exterior + interior), keeper character, boat, props,
storm sky. All original — no copyrighted assets. (Blender 5.2.2 at
C:/Users/agent/work/apps/blender-5.2.2-linux-x64/blender)

STEP 4 — UNREAL BUILD PHASE (or Godot, per Step 1's verdict):
Third-person controller, storm/weather system, the JOB-MATTERS
mechanics (lens -> beam range, oil rationing -> storm survival,
unreported wrecks -> future reefs), keeper-record auditable log,
save/load, menus, tutorial, settings. The 7 pblocks steer: director
(vision), level-content (arcs), visual (art), performance (frame
budget), balance (duty economy), qa-critic (the 8.5 judgment),
designer (lead).

STEP 5 — CRITIC LOOP:
Round = play the game -> screenshot from multiple viewpoints ->
your self-score AND qa-critic score -> binding = LOWER of the two ->
8.5+ = PASS; below = ranked issue list -> fixes -> re-round.
Up to 3 rounds (expect ~4h per iteration). Each round's scores +
issue list + diff logged. 3 rounds spent without 8.5 = honest
3-strikes report (scores, issues, what remains) — NO fake shipping.

STEP 6 — DELIVERY:
Playable build + scored screenshots + the keeper-record demo.
Everything committed. Status updated.

content:
1|# THE KEEPER'S LEDGER — DESIGN DOC (SPEC LOCK v1.0)
2|Date: 2026-10-20. Engine: Unreal 5.8.3 (Step 1 verdict: PASS, 52fps steady @1080p medium, T1000).
3|Owner: gamedesigner (LEAD). One owner per decision; decisions log and stick [game_director:5666e7d38315].
4|Status: LOCKED for build. Changes require a dated entry in section 17 (Changelog).
5|
6|---
7|
8|## 1. VISION (game_director seat)
9|
10|**One line: The job is the story.**
11|
12|You are the last keeper of a storm-ravaged island lighthouse. The keepers before you
13|vanished, one by one. The supply boat stopped coming. Every night a storm tests the
14|light; every day the island shows you what last night cost — and what the keepers
15|before you left behind.
16|
17|Pillars (in priority order — when in doubt, cut toward the top):
18|1. **Every duty has mechanical weight.** Nothing is decorative. If a duty doesn't
19|   change a number that matters, it doesn't ship.
20|2. **The island remembers.** Wrecks, damage, erosion, reefs — the island is the
21|   history of your playthrough, physically.
22|3. **The record is the story.** No dialogue choices. An auditable log of duties done
23|   and skipped decides what the inspector reads and which ending you earn.
24|4. **The storm is the antagonist.** Procedural, readable, fair. It has tells. It
25|   never cheats.
26|
27|Tone: quiet dread + competence fantasy. The Papers, Please precedent: mechanics carry
28|the meaning; you live in the world your decisions produced.
29|
30|Name-promise check [game_director:76c0c46d67f3]: "The Keeper's Ledger" promises a
31|keeper's job AND a ledger that matters. The build delivers exactly these two things.
32|Feature creep is the enemy; anything not in this doc is out of scope.
33|
34|## 2. CORE LOOP (gamedesigner seat)
35|
36|**Cycle = one Day + one Night. Target 12–18 real minutes. A full run = 12 cycles + ending (~3h).**
37|
38|### DAY (work phase)
39|1. **Read the night's report** at the log desk: what the beam did, which ships passed
40|   or were lost, what failed, what washed ashore.
41|2. **Duties** (each maps to mechanics — see section 3):
42|   - Load oil / set the ration
43|   - Clean the lens (clarity), repair the mechanism (rotation + wick feed)
44|   - Salvage wrecks on Wreck Shore (parts, oil)
45|   - Report wrecks at the chart house (marks them on the chart, prevents reefs)
46|   - Maintain paths (drainage) where storms eroded them
47|   - Keep the log (write the day's entry — feeds the record's completeness)
48|3. **Explore** for the five traces of the previous keepers (optional, story-critical).
49|4. **Light the lamp at dusk.** The night then runs on what you actually loaded, set,
50|   cleaned, and repaired. No take-backs.
51|
52|### NIGHT (storm phase)
53|- A procedural storm rolls in (section 4). The beam runs autonomously from your day's work.
54|- You may move through the tower at night: trim the wick, nudge the ration, restart a
55|  stalled mechanism — physical interventions under time pressure, not menus.
56|- Ships spawn on lanes and resolve against your beam's real reach, the real fog, and
57|  the real hazard map (including reefs your unreported wrecks became).
58|- Outcomes post to the ledger at dawn: PASSED / TURNED AWAY / WRECKED.
59|
60|### DAWN
61|Results post. Damage persists. New wrecks may have washed ashore. Autosave (diegetic:
62|"the log is written"). The island shows its memory.
63|
64|## 3. THE JOB-MATTERS SYSTEMS (anti-decoration law — the heart of the game)
65|
66|### 3.1 OIL ECONOMY (game_balance_economist seat)
67|- Oil is the single survival resource. Sources: salvage from wrecks (barrels), a finite
68|  island reserve in the shed, no resupply (the boat is gone — that's the story).
69|- **Burn rate = f(flame height).** You set flame height: higher = longer reach, more burn.
70|- **Ration:** you set the night's ration at the tank. Tank capacity is finite; the
71|  ration decides how long the light holds.
72|- **Dark interval:** if oil hits zero mid-storm, the beam dies for as long as the oil
73|  stays at zero. Every ship in fog during a dark interval is at maximum risk. The
74|  record logs the interval to the minute.
75|- Tradeoff: burn bright (save ships, drain reserve) vs ration (risk dark intervals).
76|  Storm fury is random enough that neither pure strategy dominates [game_balance_economist:0b5d7f574911].
77|
78|### 3.2 LENS → BEAM REACH
79|- **Clarity 0–100%:** salt crust and soot accumulate daily; cleaning restores it.
80|  Clarity multiplies effective reach, and fog is the storm's main weapon — so lens
81|  work is literally ships-saved.
82|- **Alignment:** mechanism wear degrades alignment; repair restores it.
83|- **Cracks:** neglect clarity below 20% for two nights and the lens cracks — a
84|  permanent reach penalty until repaired with lens parts salvaged from wrecks.
85|
86|### 3.3 MECHANISM (rotation + wick feed)
87|- The lens assembly rotates; the flash characteristic is how ships identify the light.
88|  Wear → rotation stalls → steady beam → ships misread it in rain.
89|- Wick feed jams → flame dips → dark intervals even with oil in the tank.
90|- Both repaired with clockwork/gears salvaged from wrecks. Wear is visible (wobble,
91|  tick irregularity — audio tells before failure).
92|
93|### 3.4 WRECKS → REEFS (the remembering island)
94|- Storms wash wrecks ashore (hull sections, cargo, oil barrels, sometimes a crew's
95|  belongings — story material).
96|- Each wreck must be **salvaged** (parts + oil) AND **reported** at the chart house.
97|- **Unreported wreck = unmarked hazard.** Later storms push it off the shore into the
98|  approach lanes; it becomes a reef that wrecks future ships. The island literally
99|  accumulates your neglect as new dangers on the map.
100|- Reported wrecks get a buoy (built from salvage) — marked, safe, visible.
101|- Island holds max 6 wreck sites. Each unreported one raises ship-loss odds in every
102|  later storm. This is the game's memory made physical.
103|
104|### 3.5 THE KEEPER RECORD (auditable log — the story spine)
105|- Every duty done or skipped posts a timestamped, categorized entry:
106|  LAMP / LENS / MECHANISM / WRECKS / LOG / ISLAND.
107|- Entries are **facts, not judgments**: "Night 4: dark interval 47 min. 2 ships unaccounted."
108|- The record is a real serialized data structure (in the save file), viewable in-game
109|  as the ledger book.
110|- **The inspector reads it** at the end (section 6). The ending is arithmetic on the
111|  record — no hidden flags, no dialogue.
112|- **The five traces** (previous keepers) each show THEIR record fragment: what they
113|  neglected, what it cost. The mystery assembles from records — yours and theirs.
114|  The truth: each keeper broke under the same job; the sea took them when their
115|  records failed. No monsters. The horror is the ledger.
116|- **Story-emerges-from-sim guarantee:** trace texts reference duty categories and
117|  consequences, never player-specific state they can't know — so the story cannot
118|  contradict the sim, because it is made of the sim's own data.
119|
120|### 3.6 SHIPS (the score)
121|- Ships spawn on 2–3 approach lanes per night; count scales with fury and cycle.
122|- Resolution per ship: sees the beam (reach × clarity × alignment vs fog) → holds a
123|  safe course; else risk roll against hazards (rocks, unreported reefs, drifting wrecks).
124|- Outcomes: PASSED / TURNED AWAY (safe, no credit) / WRECKED (distress flare at night;
125|  the wreck washes ashore next day — and waits for your report).
126|- You never talk to ships. Flares, bells, and the beam are the only voices.
127|
128|## 4. STORM SYSTEM (procedural)
129|- Parameters: fury 1–5, wind direction/speed, rain density, fog density, duration,
130|  gust events, lightning strikes.
131|- **Seeded:** storm seed = run_seed + cycle → deterministic per run (reproducible for
132|  QA and for the critic rubric).
133|- Fury curve across 12 cycles (escalation with breather valleys [game_level_content_designer:bb3570f4e15b]):
134|  `1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 4, 5, 3, 5, 5` — tuned by balance seat; breathers before spikes.
135|- Gusts above threshold damage the mechanism, crack the lens path, erode paths.
136|- Lightning = flash light + synthesized thunder. **No VolumetricCloud actors** (Step 1
137|  budget law: 15ms GPU). Storm sky = volumetric fog + SkyAtmosphere + rain particles.
138|
139|## 5. ISLAND LAYOUT (game_level_content_designer seat)
140|One island, five regions, walkable end-to-end in ~4–6 minutes. No fast travel (the
141|walk is short and the island IS the game).
142|
143|1. **Lighthouse Point** (center-south, high ground): the tower — lamp room (lens,
144|   mechanism, tank), keeper's room below (log desk, record book, bed).
145|2. **Cottage Row** (east): cottage, supply shed (finite starting stock), signal post.
146|3. **Wreck Shore** (west): where the sea returns what it takes; salvage bench.
147|4. **Old Landing** (north): the pier, the supply boat's last mooring (story), the
148|   chart house (wreck chart + report desk).
149|5. **The Back Hills** (south): the five trace sites of the vanished keepers, hidden in
150|   weather and terrain; a spring; the old path.
151|
152|**Paths erode:** storm gusts damage the main path (mud, rockfall). Eroded path = slow
153|travel until you maintain it (drainage duty). The island's geography carries your
154|history [game_level_content_designer:bb3570f4e15b].
155|
156|**Secret density:** traces reward exploration, never gate the core loop
157|[game_level_content_designer:88b0470741a8]. You can finish all 12 cycles without
158|finding a single trace — and get a worse ending for it, honestly earned.
159|
160|**Late-game anti-grind:** cycles 9–12 mutate the job with what the island has become
161|(new reefs you made or marked, eroded or maintained paths, wreck sites open or
162|cleared) — the late game is your history demanding attention, not the same loop
163|harder [game_level_content_designer:c811113b62ec — avoid repetitive grind samey].
164|
165|## 6. ENDINGS (branch on the record — no dialogue choices)
166|Cycle 13, dawn: the inspector's boat finally arrives. They walk the island and read
167|the ledger. The ending is **derived arithmetic on the record**:
168|
169|Inputs: ships_saved, ships_lost, dark_interval_minutes, wrecks_reported/unreported,
170|traces_found (0–5), mechanism_failures, log_completeness (0–100%).
171|
172|| Ending | Condition (shape) | Beat |
173||---|---|---|
174|| **A. The Light Holds** | high saved, few dark intervals, all wrecks reported, log complete | The inspector re-staffs the light. You train the next keeper. |
175|| **B. The Ledger and the Sea** | solid record, some gaps | The inspector takes the ledger for the archive; you stay on. Bittersweet. |
176|| **C. The Quiet Resignation** | poor record, but honest log | Relieved of duty, alive. The light dims behind you. |
177|| **D. Another Name in the Ledger** | poor record, gaps, unreported wrecks, long dark intervals | The inspector reads your record the way we read the vanished keepers'. The island keeps its next trace. |
178|| **E. The Truth Assembled** (secret) | all 5 traces + a record that answers them | The full story of the keepers, assembled from their records and yours. |
179|
180|Each ending: the inspector's walk (scripted), ledger entries read as on-screen text
181|(no VO), one final shot of the light — burning or dark. No dialogue choices anywhere.
182|
183|## 7. TUTORIAL (cycle 1 = diegetic onboarding)
184|- Cycle 1 storm is fury 1 (gentle). The previous keeper's final note guides you:
185|  a short note at each work station teaches exactly one duty, in the world.
186|- No wall-of-text. No UI tutorial overlay beyond control hints.
187|- Accessibility day one: rebindable keys, camera distance option, subtitles for all
188|  diegetic text [gamedesigner:299af5f81d60 — the options themselves are the law; that
189|  case's failure was the crash loop, which our zero-error gate covers].
190|
191|## 8. SAVE / LOAD (performance seat law)
192|- **Save anywhere** outside the storm-critical window; checkpoints justify themselves
193|  (dawn autosave is diegetic: the log is written) [gamedesigner:25ec01749aa9].
194|- **Serialized off-thread, atomic write (tmp + rename), size capped <5MB**
195|  [game_performance_engineer:32de12d63ae9, cb56bfc3e8bb, 35e6436f27c1, a3a5a32d5781, 46f8a3d79c59].
196|- Save contains: full world state, keeper record, island memory (wrecks/reefs/erosion),
197|  storm seed state, cycle counter. Loading restores exactly.
198|- Autosave at every dawn + manual save at the log desk. Single slot + backup.
199|
200|<!-- PART 2 below -->
201|
202|## 9. ART DIRECTION (game_visual_direction seat)
203|**Look: painterly-realist, storm-muted, one warm light.**
204|- Palette: cold slate blues/greens (sea, rain, rock), warm amber (the lamp, the hearth,
205|  oil). The lamp is the only saturated warm source in the world — the player's eye
206|  learns to find it, and to fear its absence.
207|- **Readability first** [game_visual_direction:6cc7f93959c6]: at gameplay distance,
208|  interactables read via shape + subtle emissive rim; hazards (rocks, reefs) read via
209|  white water even in rain. The beam must always be legible as a volume.
210|- **The one-screenshot rule** [game_visual_direction:95ad438b650f, 6f6cdeb763ba]: the
211|  key art frame is the lamp room at night, storm behind the glass, beam cutting fog
212|  over black water. Every vista in the game must sell the game in one frame.
213|- Screenshake only from authored impacts (lightning strike, hull crack, gust hitting
214|  the gallery) — never global ambient wobble [game_visual_direction:9711bf681caa].
215|- Lighting: Lumen GI (verified in Step 1), dim cool key (overcast), lamp as hero light.
216|  Interior = single warm practicals. No volumetric clouds (budget law).
217|- Materials: procedural Blender textures baked to simple maps; no AI-generated images
218|  anywhere. Grain/vignette subtle in post.
219|
220|## 10. AUDIO (studio v3 — synthesized, real DSP, no AI slop)
221|- Storm bed: filtered noise wind (gust-modulated), rain layers by density, thunder
222|  synthesized (noise burst → convolution), sea loop by fury.
223|- Diegetic: lamp hiss, mechanism tick (irregular when worn — the audio tell), bell
224|  buoy, flare crack, hull groans, pen on paper at the log desk.
225|- Music: none during play. One motif for the inspector's walk and endings.
226|- All SFX via studio v3 API (api_v3_fx.py) → WAV → UE import. Provenance: synthesized.
227|
228|## 11. PERFORMANCE BUDGET (game_performance_engineer seat — the 30fps reality)
229|Target: **1080p, medium, ≥30fps steady on T1000 4GB** (Step 1 measured 52fps headroom).
230|
231|| Line | Budget |
232||---|---|
233|| Base scene (island, tower, props) | ~19ms GPU (measured) |
234|| Volumetric fog (storm) | included above (measured) |
235|| Rain particles (GPU sprites, capped 2k) | ≤1.5ms |
236|| Lightning flash (dynamic light, rare) | ≤0.5ms amortized |
237|| Beam light + volumetric shaft | ≤2.0ms |
238|| Ships (max 3 concurrent, simple) | ≤1.0ms |
239|| Character + anims | ≤0.5ms |
240|| UI (ledger book, HUD) | ≤0.5ms |
241|| **Total worst-case** | **~26ms → 38fps floor; target 33ms → 30fps guaranteed** |
242|
243|Laws: no VolumetricCloud actors (15ms measured). No Lumen HW ray tracing. VSM on.
244|Texture pool capped. Save serialized off-thread, atomic, <5MB
245|[game_performance_engineer:32de12d63ae9]. Every build runs the smoke suite
246|[game_qa_critic:3ba945b1661e]: boot → new game → one duty → save → load → exit clean.
247|
248|## 12. BALANCE SHEET (game_balance_economist seat — the duty economy)
249|Numbers v1 (tune in playtests; every change logged in section 17):
250|
251|- **Oil:** tank 100 units. Burn = flame_height(0.5–1.5) × 6 units/hour-of-night.
252|  Night = 8 game-hours. Full flame full night = 48 units. Ration caps the night's burn.
253|- **Oil sources:** wreck barrels 15–25 each (1–2 per storm); shed reserve 120 total
254|  (finite — the clock of the run); no other source. Total economy ≈ 120 + ~10 barrels
255|  ≈ enough for ~26 night-equivalents at full flame — scarcity is real by cycle 8+.
256|- **Lens clarity:** decays 8–15%/day (storm-dependent). Cleaning = 1 day-duty, full restore.
257|  Reach multiplier = 0.4 + 0.6×clarity. Crack penalty −25% until repaired (2 lens parts).

259|  Repair = 1 day-duty + 1 clockwork part.
260|- **Wrecks:** 0–2 wash ashore per storm. Salvage = 1 duty each. Report = 1 duty each.
261|  Unreported wreck: +8% ship-loss odds per storm per wreck (compounding, max 6 wrecks).
262|- **Ships:** 2–5 per night by fury. Base loss odds 12% in fury-3 fog with healthy beam;
263|  scales with (fog × (1−reach) × hazards).
264|- **Paths:** erosion events per storm; eroded path = 2× travel time until maintained.
265|- **Traces:** 5 total; each requires reaching its site (weather-gated, not skill-gated).

reasoning_content:
Key findings:
1. No clang anywhere on the system — C++ game module compilation is not feasible without installing a toolchain (UE Linux builds require clang 19+ typically, and UE ships its own toolchain only for Android/Windows; Linux host builds need system clang). Installing clang via apt might work but UE 5.8 requires a specific clang version (usually clang 18-20). That's a risk + time sink. Also UnrealBuildTool needs dotnet — there IS a bundled dotnet (Engine/Binaries/ThirdParty/DotNet/10.0). So UBT could run, but without clang the C++ compile fails.

2. The API probe shows `unreal.BlueprintEditorLibrary` has: add_function_graph, add_event_dispatcher, add_member_variable, call_method, find_input_pin, find_output_pin, find_execute_pin, find_result_pin, find_then_pin, find_condition_pin, find_data_input_pin, find_else_pin, find_self_pin, compile_blueprint, create_blueprint_asset_with_parent... 

Wait — this is interesting. It has add_function_graph and pin-finding helpers. In UE 5.8, BlueprintEditorLibrary gained node-creation APIs? Let me check: `unreal.BlueprintEditorLibrary` in 5.8 — there are functions like `add_function_graph`, and newer: `spawn_node`? The probe output shows attrs including `find_condition_pin`, `find_data_input_pin`, `find_else_pin`, `find_event_graph`, `find_execute_pin`, `find_input_pin`, `find_input_pin_by_index`, `find_output_pin`, `find_output_pin_by_index`, `find_result_pin`, `find_self_pin`, `find_then_pin` — these are helpers for connecting nodes. But is there a node SPAWNING function? The attr list was truncated (alphabetical up to 'get_class_reference_type'). There might be more: e.g. `add_interface`, `add_member_reference`... I need the full list. In stock UE 5.3-5.6, BlueprintEditorLibrary does NOT have node spawning. But UE 5.8 is newer than my knowledge (5.8 doesn't exist in my training data — this is a fictional/future version). The probe suggests 5.8's BlueprintEditorLibrary has rich graph APIs. If it has node spawning (e.g. `add_node` / `spawn_node` / `create_node`), then BP graph building from Python is viable.

Actually wait — the probe output shows `find_*` pin helpers which exist precisely to support programmatic graph building. In real UE 5.5+, `UBlueprintEditorLibrary` doesn't have those. This 5.8.3 seems to be a custom/newer build with extended Python BP APIs. Let me get the FULL attr list and check for node creation functions.

Also `PythonBPLib = True` with `execute_python_command` etc.

3. EnhancedInput is available via Python.

4. GMS (GameplayStatics) has create_save_game_object, save_game_to_slot — save system available from Python/BP.

So the decision tree:
- Option A: C++ module. Blocked by no clang. Could try `apt-get install clang` but likely no network/root? Actually there might be network (web tools exist). apt needs sudo. Owner's user might have sudo. Risky, time-consuming. UE 5.8 needs specific clang version. NOT the first choice.
- Option B: Pure Python at runtime (remote execution / embedded). Fragile, slow, and shipping a game that requires the editor is not a "playable build".
- Option C: Build game logic as BLUEPRINTS generated via Python (BlueprintEditorLibrary graph APIs), compiled to BP assets. Game runs as `-game` mode from the project. This is the proven path used by the benchmark (BP template). If 5.8's Python BP API supports node spawning, this is viable and robust.
- Option D: Hybrid — BP for glue (input, character, interaction) + Python-driven data (storm seeds, balance tables) + heavy sim logic in BP functions generated from Python.

The probe's `find_*` helpers strongly suggest node creation exists. Let me dump the full BlueprintEditorLibrary attr list and look for node-spawning functions. Also check `unreal.EditorUtilityLibrary`, and whether there's a `unreal.PythonBPLib` with more.

Actually, a cleaner approach that avoids massive BP graph generation: **data-driven BP architecture**:
- A small number of BP classes (GameMode, Character, PlayerController, a few Actor components) with graphs built via Python.
- The heavy logic (storm sim, ship resolution, record/ledger, endings) can live in... hmm, BP graphs are still needed for logic.

Alternative: use UE's built-in systems maximally:
- Level scripting via LevelSequence? No.
- Data assets + BP functions.

Honestly, if BlueprintEditorLibrary can spawn nodes and wire pins, I can generate BP graphs programmatically — it's verbose but deterministic and testable. The sim logic (storm, ships, record) is mostly arithmetic + timers — very expressible as BP function graphs (pure functions + event graphs).

Let me first get the full attr list of BlueprintEditorLibrary and check for node creation. Also check `unreal.BlueprintEditorLibrary` docs signature via help().

Also — check if there's a `unreal.EditorPythonScriptingLibrary` with `run_python_command` at runtime... For the game runtime, Python CAN be enabled at runtime (force_enable_python_at_runtime attr seen in pylib!). That's a fallback: ship the game with runtime Python enabled and drive logic from .py files. But runtime Python in a packaged game is heavy; for a `-game` editor-binary run it's fine (we're not packaging a standalone binary — "playable build" = runs via UnrealEditor-Cmd -game, which is how the benchmark ran).

Actually wait — what IS the deliverable "playable build"? Given no package toolchain issues (packaging Linux needs the same toolchain for cooking? Cooking doesn't need clang; packaging a Linux game DOES need clang to compile the game module — but a BP-only project packages without compiling C++... actually packaging always compiles the project module if Source exists; BP-only projects don't have Source, so packaging works without clang!). But packaging also needs UnrealPak etc. — those are prebuilt binaries, fine. However packaging takes long and needs StageDirectory. A `-game` run from the editor binary with a cooked... no, -game from editor binary runs uncooked. That's how the benchmark ran (UnrealEditor-Cmd ScalTest.uproject -game). That's a legitimate playable build for this exercise: "runs, playable start to finish, exits cleanly".

So the architecture decision:
**BP-only project, gameplay logic in Blueprints generated by Python via BlueprintEditorLibrary (if node spawning exists), heavy data in Python-generated DataTables/DataAssets, run via UnrealEditor-Cmd -game.**

If node spawning does NOT exist: fallback is C++ via apt clang (risky) or... hmm, actually there's another path: **UE's "Blueprint Macros/Functions via text"** — no. Or **Python runtime plugin** (ScriptPlugin) — the engine may include the PythonScriptPlugin which supports runtime execution (we saw force_enable_python_at_runtime). With runtime Python, the game logic can be Python classes registered as... but exposing Python to gameplay actors at runtime requires the PythonScriptPlugin in game mode (it works: -game with PythonScriptPlugin enabled can execute Python and Python can spawn actors, bind input via PythonScriptGameSubsystem... in real UE, `unreal.PythonBPLib`... hmm, actually there IS `unreal.PythonScriptGameSubsystem` in newer versions with execute_python_command and you can hook Tick via delegates? Delegates from Python at runtime are possible (bind_event_dynamic). It's fragile but real.

{"content": "# Probe UE 5.8.3 Python API: full BlueprintEditorLibrary surface + node creation + runtime python
import unreal, os

REPORT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "logs", "api_probe2.txt")
lines = []
def note(m):
    lines.append(m)
    unreal.log("[PROBE2] %s" % m)

# 1. Full BlueprintEditorLibrary attrs
bpl = unreal.BlueprintEditorLibrary
attrs = sorted(dir(bpl))
note("BPL_FULL_BEGIN")
for a in attrs:
    try:
        fn = getattr(bpl, a)
        if callable(fn):
            try:
                note("  %s%s" % (a, str(inspect_sig := getattr(fn, "__doc__", ""))[:0] or ""))
            except Exception:
                pass
    except Exception:
        pass
# simpler: just list names
note("BPL_ATTRS: " + ", ".join(attrs))
note("BPL_FULL_END")

# 2. doc signatures for the interesting ones
for name in ["add_function_graph", "add_member_variable", "compile_blueprint",
             "create_blueprint_asset_with_parent", "call_method", "add_event_dispatcher",
             "find_execute_pin", "find_input_pin", "find_output_pin", "find_then_pin",
             "find_self_pin", "find_result_pin", "find_condition_pin", "find_data_input_pin",
             "find_else_pin", "find_event_graph", "find_input_pin_by_index", "find_output_pin_by_index"]:
    fn = getattr(bpl, name, None)
    if fn:
        note("SIG %s :: %s" % (name, (fn.__doc__ or "no doc").replace("\n", " | ")[:400]))

# 3. node creation hunt across likely libraries
for libname in ["BlueprintEditorLibrary", "EditorUtilityLibrary", "EditorAssetLibrary",
                "PythonBPLib", "KismetSystemLibrary", "KismetLibrary", "AssetToolsHelpers"]:
    try:
        lib = getattr(unreal, libname, None)
        if lib is None:
            continue
        hits = [a for a in dir(lib) if any(k in a.lower() for k in ("node", "spawn", "wire", "link", "connect", "pin", "graph", "schema"))]
        if hits:
            note("NODEHUNT %s: %s" % (libname, ", ".join(sorted(hits))))
    except Exception as e:
        note("NODEHUNT %s err %s" % (libname, e))

# 4. any class with 'node' in name
node_classes = [c for c in dir(unreal) if "node" in c.lower() and ("graph" in c.lower() or "blueprint" in c.lower() or "ed" in c.lower())]
note("NODE_CLASSES: " + ", ".join(node_classes[:40]))

# 5. runtime python check
try:
    note("runtime_py_available=%s" % unreal.PythonBPLib is not None)
except Exception:
    pass
for sub in ["PythonScriptGameSubsystem", "PythonScriptLibrary"]:
    note("has %s = %s" % (sub, hasattr(unreal, sub)))

# 6. EnhancedInput details
ei = [c for c in dir(unreal) if "InputMapping" in c or "InputAction" in c]
note("ENHANCED_INPUT_CLASSES: " + ", ".join(sorted(ei)[:30]))

# 7. save game
note("SaveGame class: %s" % hasattr(unreal, "SaveGameObject"))

# 8. widget / UMG creation from python
umg = [c for c in dir(unreal) if c.startswith("Widget")][:25]
note("UMG_CLASSES: " + ", ".join(umg))

with open(REPORT, "w") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(lines))
note("report written: %s" % REPORT)
", "path": "tools/ue_api_probe2.py"}

content:
The probe reveals the decisive architecture facts:
- **Blueprint graph node authoring is NOT exposed** (only find/list/pin-read APIs) — so gameplay logic can't be BP-graph-built from Python
- **No clang toolchain** — C++ module path is out
- **`PythonScriptLibrary` exists + `PythonBPLib` with `force_enable_python_at_runtime`** — runtime Python is the viable path
- Template ThirdPerson content (character + input BPs) already in ScalTest — movement comes free

The make-or-break test: **does Python execute and run timer-driven callbacks in `-game` mode?** That decides everything. Building the runtime probe:
reasoning_content:
Key findings:
1. `BlueprintEditorLibrary` has graph READ APIs (find pins, list graphs) but I don't see node CREATION APIs (no `spawn_node`, no `create_node`, no `link_pin`/`connect_pin`). NODEHUNT shows only find/list/set_pos functions. So **building Blueprint graphs from Python is NOT feasible** — you can add graphs and variables, but not spawn nodes or wire them.

2. `PythonScriptLibrary` exists (runtime python execution!). That's huge: `unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command` — but that's editor-side. For RUNTIME (in-game), there's no PythonScriptGameSubsystem. Hmm.

3. No SaveGameObject class directly, but `unreal.GameplayStatics.create_save_game_object` exists (from first probe: "GMS attrs = ['create_save_game_object', 'does_save_game_exist', 'open_level', 'open_level_by_soft_object_ptr', 'save_game_to_slot']").

So the architecture decision crystallizes:

**Blueprint graphs cannot be authored from Python** (no node-spawn API). **C++ has no compiler toolchain** (no clang). What's left for gameplay logic?

Option A: **Engine-side systems via existing BP classes + level scripting**: Level Sequence + triggers... too weak for the sim.

Option B: **Python at runtime via a different mechanism**: UE supports "Remote Execution" of Python (PythonScriptPlugin settings: remote execution multicast). But that requires an editor instance running. For a packaged game, no.

Wait — actually, let me reconsider. The critical question: does the DELIVERABLE need to be a packaged build, or a playable build run from the editor? The brief says "Playable build + scored screenshots + the keeper-record demo." Running from UnrealEditor-Cmd -game mode IS playable (that's how the benchmark ran). So the game can ship as "run via editor-cmd -game" — that's how it was verified in Step 1.

In -game mode launched from the editor binary, is Python available? The PythonScriptPlugin can be enabled for runtime... Actually there IS a way: `unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command` works in editor context. In -game mode (launched via UnrealEditor-Cmd -game), the editor modules ARE loaded (it's the editor binary in game mode), so PythonScriptPlugin should be active and Python should work!

That's the architecture:
- **Game mode logic in Python, executed at runtime via the PythonScriptPlugin** in editor-cmd -game mode.
- How does Python code run every tick in game mode? Options:
  a. A level blueprint that calls into Python... but we can't author BP graphs.
  b. Python can register delegates/timers: `unreal.register_python_callback`? There's the `unreal.PythonScriptLibrary` and also the ability to spawn actors from Python and attach... hmm, but tick callbacks?
  
  Actually UE Python has: `unreal.register_slate_post_tick_callback(callback)` — editor only. For game mode... there's `unreal.Actor.bind_event`? Python can subclass `unreal.Actor`? No — Python can't define new UObject classes at runtime in stock UE (that's what the `unreal.PythonBPLib` third-party plugin does, not stock).

Hmm wait — actually stock UE Python CAN do this: you can create a Python-defined class deriving from `unreal.Object`? No. Stock UE Python does not support defining new UClasses.

BUT: there's a well-known pattern — **Python-driven actors via existing engine classes + delegates**:
- `unreal.Actor` has `receive_tick`? Not bindable from Python directly.
- Timer handles: `unreal.TimerHandle`... Python can't set timers on itself without an object.

Hmm, actually there IS a documented pattern: `unreal.get_engine().add_event_handler`? No.

Let me think about what's actually available:
1. `unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command(command)` — executes Python in the game thread. In -game mode with the plugin enabled, this works (the plugin's execution path is the same).
2. Delegates: many engine delegates are exposed to Python and CAN be bound from Python: e.g., `unreal.ActorOnClicked`, `unreal.TimerHandle`... The key one: **FTimerManager timers can be set from Python** via `unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate`! Yes: `unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate()` + `bind_callable` (or bind_ufunction), then `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer_for_time_and_next(delegate, time, looping)`. Hmm — actually it's `unreal.KismetSystemLibrary.k2_set_timer...`? The exposed function is `unreal.GameplayStatics`... no. It's `TimerManager` — not directly exposed. But `unreal.KismetSystemLibrary` has `K2_SetTimer`? That's C++-only. The Python-exposed path: `unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate` + `actor.set_timer_by_time_and_next`? Hmm, `AActor` doesn't have SetTimer; that's on TimerManager or on `UUserWidget`...

Actually the cleanest documented Python pattern for ticking:
```python
import unreal
def my_tick():
    ...
unreal.register_python_callback(...)  # doesn't exist
```

Known-good: **`unreal.SlateApplication` post-tick** — editor only.

For GAME mode, the documented approach in Epic's docs ("Scripting the Editor using Python") is editor-focused. BUT there's a classic trick used by many UE python games/tools: spawn an actor with a **TimelineComponent**? Or use `unreal.ActorComponent` delegates?

Alternative robust approach: **drive the game loop from a Level Sequence**? Ugly.

Wait — much better idea: **`unreal.EngineSubsystem`/world tick delegates**: `unreal.World` exposes `on_actor_moved`? no...

Hmm, let me recall actual UE Python API: there IS `unreal.register_python_callback(name, callable)` and `unreal.execute_python_command`. And crucially there's **`unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command`** which can be called FROM Blueprint via the "Execute Python Command" node — but we can't author BP graphs...

OK here's another angle — **the tick problem solved by an existing engine actor**: `unreal.AmbientSound`? No. What about spawning a `unreal.TimelineHelper`? 

Actually! The simplest: **`unreal.GameplayStatics.create_save_game_object`** proves GameplayStatics functions are callable. GameplayStatics doesn't have timers. But **`unreal.SystemLibrary`** (UKismetSystemLibrary) — does it have `K2_SetTimer`? In UE 5.x, `UKismetSystemLibrary::K2_SetTimer` is BlueprintCallable! Yes: "K2_SetTimer (Object object, string function_name, float time, bool looping...)" — it's exposed as `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer(object, function_name, time, looping, ...)`. And the object can be ANY UObject with a UFUNCTION... but Python objects aren't UObjects.

Hmm, but `TimerDynamicDelegate` binds to a PYTHON callable: `unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate()` then `.bind_callable(python_function)`. And `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer_for_time_and_next(delegate, time, looping)`? Let me check the actual name: In UE Python it's `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer(delegate, time, looping)`? I recall `UKismetSystemLibrary::K2_SetTimerForTimeAndNext`... not sure.

I should just PROBE it: check `dir(unreal.SystemLibrary)` for timer functions, and test `unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate` binding a Python callable, in -game mode. That's the make-or-break test for the whole architecture. If dynamic delegate timers work in -game mode, the game loop is: Python module + timer-driven tick + engine classes for everything else (movement via existing Character class configured by Python, input via Enhanced Input... hmm, input binding from Python?).

INPUT is the next hard problem: third-person controller needs WASD → movement. Enhanced Input actions need BP graph wiring (K2Node_EnhancedInputAction) — can't author. BUT: the TP_ThirdPerson template project (game/ScalTest has ThirdPerson content! `Content/ThirdPerson/Blueprints/BP_ThirdPersonCharacter.uasset` etc.) — the template's BP_ThirdPersonCharacter ALREADY HAS input wired (Enhanced Input with IMC_Default, IA_Move, IA_Look, IA_Jump). The ScalTest project already contains the full ThirdPerson template content with working character BP + input! That's why it was chosen. So movement/look/jump come free from the template BP.

Then Python's job: game systems (oil, lens, storm, ships, record, save) driven by timers + interacting with the world via engine APIs (spawn actors, move them, lights, materials, HUD via UMG widgets created from Python? UMG widget creation from Python: `unreal.WidgetBlueprintLibrary.create(widget_class, owning_player)` — needs a WidgetBlueprint class asset... which we can't author graphs for. BUT `unreal.UserWidget`... hmm, can Python create a UserWidget subclass? No.

HUD alternative: **`unreal.DebugText` / on-screen messages** (KismetSystemLibrary.print_string) — works but ugly. Better: **UMG via pre-made WidgetBlueprint assets**? Can't author.

Hmm wait — actually there's another UI path: **`unreal.CanvasPanel`...** no, needs a widget blueprint.

What about **`unreal.HUD` class + drawing via canvas**? AHUD::DrawText etc. are not BlueprintCallable... some are (DrawText is BlueprintCallable? In UE5, `DrawText` on HUD is BlueprintCallable? I believe `UHUD::DrawText` IS BlueprintCallable — yes, HUD draw functions are exposed to BP).

OK. I'm going deep on speculation. The right move: **probe the runtime capabilities in -game mode directly** — that's the decisive experiment:
1. Does Python run in -game mode? (execute a script at startup — how? `-run=pythonscript` is editor-only... for game mode: `-ExecutePythonScript=`? There's a command line: `UnrealEditor-Cmd proj -game -run=pythonscript`? Hmm. Actually the PythonScriptPlugin supports `-ExecutePythonScript=path` on game launch? I recall `py` console command works in game if plugin enabled. And there's `+ExecCmds="py ..."`. 

The proven launch pattern from Runner: `UnrealEditor-Cmd <proj> -game ... -ExecCmds="FPSChart"`. So ExecCmds run in game mode. Can ExecCmds run `py "import mymodule"`? The `py` console command takes the rest of the line as python code. With spaces it might work: `-ExecCmds="py import unreal; print('HELLO')"`. Commas separate multiple commands in ExecCmds... risky but testable.

Better: the PythonScriptPlugin has a setting for **startup python scripts in game**: `[/Script/PythonScriptPlugin.PythonScriptPluginSettings]` + there's also `-run=pythonscript` which works in GAME mode too? The `-run=` switch is handled by the engine's commandlet-style entry... Actually `-run=pythonscript` launches the PythonScriptCommandlet which is editor-ish. Hmm.

There IS a documented game-mode path: **`-ExecutePythonScript=`**? I'm not certain. Let me just probe: launch -game with ExecCmds py command and see if it executes. Also probe `unreal.SystemLibrary` timer functions and `TimerDynamicDelegate`.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider the whole architecture once more. There's a MUCH more robust option I haven't fully considered:

**The game logic doesn't need to live in UE at all for the sim part... no, it does — it must affect the world.**

Alternative: **Drive everything through the level + existing template BPs + Python timers**. The template BP character handles movement. Python (via timer ticks at 10-30Hz) runs the sim: storm state, oil burn, ships, record. Python manipulates: lights (unreal.DirectionalLight/SpotLight set_editor_property), fog, rain particles (spawn unreal.ParticleSystemActor? Niagara systems from template?), ships (spawn static mesh actors, move them), HUD (print_string + maybe HUD draw), save (GameplayStatics save game with a SaveGameObject class... create_save_game_object needs a SaveGame CLASS — Python can't define one. BUT there's `unreal.SaveGame` class itself! `create_save_game_object(unreal.SaveGame)` — the base class is instantiable? SaveGameObject in the first probe: "SaveGameObject = False" (no factory). `GameplayStatics.create_save_game_object(class)` — passing the BASE `unreal.SaveGame` class might work, giving a generic SaveGame object whose properties we set... but base SaveGame has no properties to store arbitrary data. Hmm — we could serialize our state to JSON STRING and store... where? There's `unreal.FileManager`? Python in UE has full `os`/file access! Python can just write JSON files to disk directly (Saved/SaveGames/). Save/load = Python json to file. That's simpler and fully under our control. The "save game" law (off-thread, atomic, capped) — Python can do atomic write (tmp+rename) easily; off-thread via a Python thread (GIL caveats, but writes are tiny).

So the architecture is viable IF:
(a) Python executes in -game mode, and
(b) timer-driven Python callbacks work in -game mode.

Both testable in one probe run. If (a) fails, fallback: launch via `-run=pythonscript` in the EDITOR binary with `-game`... which is what we're doing anyway (UnrealEditor-Cmd -game). The question is just how to bootstrap the first python execution. Options: ExecCmds py, or a startup .ini hook, or... the PythonScriptPlugin setting "remote execution" + an external driver script that connects and sends commands! Remote execution uses multicast UDP — an external Python process can send `py ...` commands to the running game. That's a solid bootstrap: game launches, external driver sends bootstrap command, game runs autonomously. But for DELIVERY, the game should run standalone without an external driver... ExecCmds bootstrap is cleaner for delivery.

Hmm, actually there's an even cleaner documented bootstrap for game mode: in DefaultEngine.ini or via command line, `py` exec... Let me look: PythonScriptPlugin has console command `py`, `pyexec` (execute a .py file by path!). `pyexec "path/to/file.py"` — THAT's the bootstrap: `-ExecCmds="pyexec /abs/path/boot.py"`. ExecCmds executes after engine init. 

One concern: ExecCmds with quotes/paths. Testable.

Also — timing: ExecCmds run early; Python plugin might not be initialized yet. There's a delay option: `-ExecCmds="Delay 5, pyexec ..."`? Delay is a console command ("Delay" exists? there's "Delay" exec in some builds). Alternatively the boot.py itself can be re-triggered... or use `py` with a tiny one-liner that schedules the real boot via a timer... but timers need the plugin working — chicken and egg. Simplest: test if ExecCmds pyexec works at all; if too early, use the remote-execution driver for dev and figure out delivery bootstrap later (there's also `PythonScriptPlugin` setting `bRemoteExecution`... and there's an ini setting for startup scripts? I don't recall one for game mode).

Hmm — one more possibility: **`unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command` called from a level blueprint**... can't author. BUT WAIT — can I author a level blueprint via the BlueprintEditorLibrary graph APIs? I established node CREATION isn't exposed... but actually, let me double-check: maybe `unreal.PythonBPLib` (the probe said "PythonBPLib = True"!) — that's NOT stock; wait, "PythonBPLib = True" in the first probe — hmm, that might be a custom plugin in this engine build? It had attrs: call_method, execute_python_command, force_enable_python_at_runtime, get_class, get_default_object... "force_enable_python_at_runtime" — interesting! That suggests this engine has a runtime-python plugin. Let me check what plugin provides PythonBPLib... Actually "PythonBPLib" might be from the "PythonScriptPlugin" as a BP library class name? Stock UE has "PythonScriptLibrary" (the probe confirmed `has PythonScriptLibrary = True`). PythonBPLib might be a third-party BP library exposed to Python. Its `execute_python_command` + `force_enable_python_at_runtime` strongly suggests RUNTIME python support exists in this build.

OK, enough analysis — the decisive probe: run -game mode, ExecCmds pyexec boot probe, which:
1. writes a receipt file (proves execution),
2. lists unreal.SystemLibrary timer functions,
3. tests TimerDynamicDelegate + Python callable firing (write receipt #2 after 1s),
4. tests GameplayStatics save + Python file IO,
5. checks unreal.PythonBPLib / PythonScriptLibrary functions,
6. tests input: does the template BP character work (can't test input headlessly without a player... skip; movement is template-proven).

If the timer test passes → architecture locked: Python-driven game in UE -game mode. Then I build the game as a Python package inside the project (Content/Python/keepers/), bootstrapped by pyexec, with the template character for movement.

Also need to verify: does -game mode with the ScalTest project load Lvl_ScalStorm (GameDefaultMap=/Game/Lvl_ScalStorm) — yes per ini. For the real game I'll build Lvl_KeepersLedger as the game map with the template character spawned (or set GameMode to use BP_ThirdPersonCharacter).

Big remaining question: the K2Node/Blueprint graph authoring — NOT needed under this architecture. 

And UMG UI: probe whether we can create widgets from pure Python. `unreal.UserWidget`... there's `unreal.WidgetBlueprintLibrary.create(world, class, player)` — with class = a WidgetBlueprint ASSET (authored). Can't author WBP graphs from Python (WidgetBlueprint is a BP with a widget tree — the tree CAN be edited via Python? `unreal.WidgetBlueprint` has `widget_tree` property! And `unreal.WidgetTree` has `root_widget`... and you can construct widgets: `unreal.WidgetBlueprintLibrary.create(...)` returns a UWidget instance; can I ADD it to a tree and save? Possibly: widget_tree.set_editor_property('root_widget', w). And set widget properties (text, color). And bind events? Delegates on widgets (OnClicked) — bind_ufunction needs a UObject method... Python callables can bind to dynamic delegates: `widget.on_clicked.add_callable(python_fn)`? If dynamic multicast delegates expose add_callable, UI interactivity works from Python!

This is all probeable. But careful: don't spend forever probing. The critical path: (a) pyexec bootstrap in -game, (b) timer ticks. UI fallback = HUD draw functions + print_string (always works). Let me also probe widget creation quickly in the same probe.

Actually, let me simplify the probe to the two make-or-break items + a couple of cheap extras, run it, and decide. Timebox: this probe run ~3-5 min.

One more consideration — VRAM/perf: -game mode with editor binary is heavier than a packaged build but Step 1 proved 52fps in exactly this mode. Fine.

Also the segfault at exit (139) in the probe run: happened AFTER report write, during engine teardown with -nullrhi. The Step 1 benchmark runs exited cleanly (exit 0) with real rendering. The nullrhi teardown segfault is likely a known quirk; for game runs we use real rendering anyway. Note it, move on.

Let me write the runtime probe now. Key detail: how to pass pyexec through ExecCmds safely. Pattern: -ExecCmds="pyexec C:/Users/agent/work/project/test-runs/test3-gamedesigner/t3-keepers-20261020-140210/tools/rt_probe.py" — absolute path, no spaces. Should be fine.

Also add a fallback inside the same run: after 10s, if receipt missing... can't self-check from inside; I'll check from shell after.

Timeout: game mode boot ~2-4min per Runner. Give 420s, and have the probe self-exit: after tests, `unreal.SystemLibrary.quit_game(...)`? For editor-cmd game mode, `quit` console command exits. From Python: `unreal.SystemLibrary.execute_console_command(world, "quit")`? Hmm, need world context — `unreal.get_editor_subsystem`... in game mode, `unreal.EditorLevelLibrary` might not work. `unreal.SystemLibrary.execute_console_command` needs a context world — Python's execute_python_command runs on game thread; getting the world: `unreal.UnrealEngine.get_world()`? Hmm, `unreal.get_engine().get_world()`? There's `unreal.EditorActorSubsystem` (editor only). For game: `unreal.GameplayStatics.get_player_controller(world, 0)` needs world. 

World access in game-mode Python: `unreal.SystemLibrary.get_default_level`? The classic: `unreal.get_editor_subsystem(unreal.UnrealEditorSubsystem)` gives `get_game_world()` in editor; in -game mode... UnrealEditorSubsystem might still exist (editor binary!). Actually simplest: `unreal.World`... Let me include several attempts in the probe and log which works:
- `unreal.get_engine()` → has `get_world?` hmm.
- PythonBPLib.get_class etc.

Known-good pattern from docs: `unreal.EditorLevelLibrary.get_game_world()`? In UE5, EditorLevelLibrary is deprecated → `unreal.UnrealEditorSubsystem().get_game_world()`. In -game mode (editor binary), subsystems load. I'll try multiple and log.

For the timer test I don't even need a world: `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer...` hmm K2_SetTimer needs an OBJECT with function. TimerDynamicDelegate route: `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer_for_time_and_next`? I'll enumerate SystemLibrary timer functions in the probe and try the delegate one.

Actually — even simpler tick source that definitely works in game mode: **`unreal.PythonScriptLibrary.execute_python_command` scheduling via console `Delay`**? no.

Hmm, what about the **actor-based approach**: spawn a plain `unreal.Actor` (spawnable from Python via world spawn_actor), then... plain Actor has no tick exposed to Python. But `unreal.ActorComponent`... no.

**The delegate that definitely exists**: `unreal.Actor` has `on_actor_begin_overlap` etc. — needs movement/collision. 

**Best bet remains TimerDynamicDelegate + KismetSystemLibrary.K2_SetTimerForTimeAndNext** — wait, actually I now recall clearly: `UKismetSystemLibrary::K2_SetTimer` (object+function) and `K2_SetTimerForTimeAndNext`... and there's `K2_SetTimerDelegate` which takes an FTimerDynamicDelegate — EXPOSED to python as `unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer_delegate(delegate, time, looping, initial_start_delay)`. And TimerDynamicDelegate binds python callables via `.bind_callable`. I'm fairly confident this works — it's the standard python timer pattern. Probe will confirm.

Let me also prepare the exit: after tests pass, execute `quit` via... `unreal.SystemLibrary.execute_console_command(None, "quit")` — context can be None? It's BlueprintCallable with context world pin — from python, passing None world might work or crash. Alternative: just let the 420s timeout SIGTERM it (Runner noted graceful SIGTERM exit is handled cleanly once startup completes). For the probe, timeout-kill is fine.

Write the probe, run it, check receipts. GO.

{"content": "# PROJECT STARTUP SCRIPT — runs automatically in -game mode AFTER map load.
# This is the Keeper's Ledger bootstrap. Receipts to logs/rt_probe.txt.
import unreal, os

BASE = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", ".."))
LOG = os.path.join(BASE, "logs", "rt_probe.txt")

def w(m):
    try:
        with open(LOG, "a") as f:
            f.write(m + "\n")
    except Exception:
        pass

w("=== INIT_UNREAL BOOTSTRAP FIRED ===")
w("engine: %s" % unreal.SystemLibrary.get_engine_version())

world = None
try:
    world = unreal.get_editor_subsystem(unreal.UnrealEditorSubsystem).get_game_world()
except Exception as e:
    w("world err: %s" % e)
w("world: %s" % world)

TICKS = {"n": 0}

def on_timer():
    TICKS["n"] += 1
    if TICKS["n"] <= 3:
        w("TIMER TICK %d" % TICKS["n"])
    if TICKS["n"] == 3:
        w("TIMER_TEST_PASS")
        # file IO + atomic json save
        try:
            save_dir = os.path.join(BASE, "game", "ScalTest", "Saved", "KeeperSaves")
            os.makedirs(save_dir, exist_ok=True)
            data = {"cycle": 1, "oil": 87.5, "record": [{"cat": "LAMP", "text": "lamp lit"}]}
            tmp = os.path.join(save_dir, "slot0.json.tmp")
            with open(tmp, "w") as f:
                json.dump(data, f)
            os.replace(tmp, os.path.join(save_dir, "slot0.json"))
            w("FILEIO_TEST_PASS")
        except Exception:
            w("FILEIO_TEST_FAIL: %s" % traceback.format_exc())
        # player controller + print
        try:
            pc = unreal.GameplayStatics.get_player_controller(world, 0)
            w("PC: %s" % pc)
            unreal.SystemLibrary.print_string(pc, "KEEPERS LEDGER RT OK", True, True,
                                              unreal.LinearColor(r=1.0, g=0.8, b=0.2, a=1.0), 8.0)
            w("PRINT_TEST_PASS")
        except Exception:
            w("PRINT_TEST_FAIL: %s" % traceback.format_exc())
        # pawn check
        try:
            pawn = unreal.GameplayStatics.get_player_pawn(world, 0)
            w("PAWN: %s" % pawn)
        except Exception:
            w("PAWN fail: %s" % traceback.format_exc())
        # quit
        unreal.SystemLibrary.execute_console_command(world, "quit")
        w("QUIT issued")

import traceback  # noqa: E402

try:
    td = unreal.TimerDynamicDelegate()
    td.bind_callable(on_timer)
    unreal.SystemLibrary.k2_set_timer_delegate(td, 0.5, True, 0.0)
    w("TIMER_ARMED")
except Exception:
    w("TIMER_ARM_FAIL: %s" % traceback.format_exc())

w("=== BOOTSTRAP SETUP DONE ===")

Let me check: in UE 5.1+, it's `unreal.PyActor` — but maybe in 5.8 they moved to `unreal.PyTestActor`? No. Actually the classes might only be registered when the plugin's content is mounted... Or they're under `unreal.PyActor` only if compiled with the plugin — the plugin IS loaded (libUnrealEditor-PythonScriptPlugin.so loaded). Hmm, but the class registration might be in a different module: "PyCore"? Let me probe dir(unreal) for anything with "Py" prefix.
- TIMER_ARMED via set_timer_delegate ✓ — but did the ticks fire? The probe file shows no TIMER TICK lines... The run was killed at 170s (EXIT=124) — startup ~2-3min means the timer had little time. The ticks would have appeared if the process ran long enough after setup. The log shows setup done; ticks pending when timeout hit.

Actually for spawning: `unreal.GameplayStatics.begin_spawning_actor_from_class(world, class, transform)` or simpler: `world.actor_spawn_actor`? The correct API in UE python: `world.spawn_actor` doesn't exist; it's `actor.spawn_actor` (on any actor, spawns child) OR `unreal.EditorAssetLibrary`... For runtime: `unreal.GameplayStatics.begin_spawning_actor_from_class` returns actor. Or `unreal.Actor.spawn_actor` — an actor method.
